first_draft.title: Alice and Bob and the Missing Mitten
first_draft.text:
Alice had a best friend named Bob, and Bob was a cat. He was a fat orange cat with one white sock and a tail that curled like a question mark. Every morning he sat on the windowsill and waited for Alice to come down the stairs.

On Saturday, Alice came down the stairs, and she did not say good morning. She stood in the kitchen with her hands empty and her lip trembling.

"My mitten is gone," she said. "The red one with the bobble on top. Grandma knitted it for me."

Bob hopped down from the windowsill. He sniffed the air with his pink nose. Then he trotted off toward the hallway, his white sock flashing like a little flag.

"Wait for me!" called Alice, and she ran after him in her socks.

Bob sniffed under the coat rack. He sniffed behind the umbrella stand. He sniffed the bottom of the big blue armchair, where a crumb of toast was hiding. Then he stopped, very still, and stared at the laundry basket. A sleepy purr rumbled out of him, which was not what Alice expected at all.

Alice tiptoed closer and lifted the lid. Inside, under a pile of warm towels, was something red with a bobble on top. Bob had not found the mitten. He had found the cozy towels, and the mitten was tangled in the middle of them, as if it had been napping too.

"Oh, Bob!" Alice giggled. "You're a terrible detective, but a wonderful nose."

Bob blinked slowly, as if he were taking a bow.

Alice pulled the mitten free and tugged it onto her hand. It fit perfectly. Then she sat down on the floor beside the basket, and Bob climbed into her lap, heavy and warm, like a bag of flour that had decided to purr.

Outside, the sky turned from gold to pink to a soft, sleepy blue. The kitchen clock ticked, tock, tock, tock. A bird sang one last small song in the garden and then went quiet.

Alice's eyes grew heavy. Bob's purr grew slow and deep. The red mitten rested on her knee, its bobble bouncing softly with each breath.

And the house settled down around them, one room at a time, until everything was still.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Rocket and the Backyard Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo pulled on his pirate hat, the one with the crooked feather, and tucked a folded map into his pocket. Rocket, his scruffy brown dog, wagged so hard that his whole back end wiggled. "Ahoy, first mate," Leo whispered. Rocket barked once, which Leo decided meant yes.

The map was drawn in purple crayon. It showed the old apple tree, the squeaky gate, and a big X beside the garden shed. Under the X, in wobbly letters, were the words: BURIED SHINY THINGS. Leo traced the X with his finger. "X marks the spot," he said. "Let's go, Rocket!"

They crept past the sandbox, where a sleepy ladybug was napping on a red spade. They tiptoed over the bumpy grass and hopped across a puddle that went splish, splash, squelch. Rocket sniffed every single leaf along the way. Snuffle, snuffle, snort! Something under the apple tree smelled interesting, and Rocket started to dig.

Dirt flew everywhere. Leo laughed and grabbed his small shovel. "Easy, Captain Rocket! We need to find the treasure without making a mud pie of the whole yard!" But the digging stopped when Rocket's nose bumped something hard. Clink! Leo knelt down and brushed away the soil. Inside a rusty tin box was a note, a bent bottle cap, and a wrapped toffee that looked very old.

"Hmm," said Leo, scratching his chin. The note was not a treasure map at all. It said: Thank you for finding my lost whistle. The whistle was missing from the tin. Leo looked all around the yard. Rocket pawed at the shed door, sniffing hard, and Leo followed him inside. There, hanging on a nail, was a silver whistle on a faded blue string.

"You found it!" Leo cheered. He gave Rocket a big hug, and Rocket licked his nose. They returned the whistle to the tin, and Leo wrote a new note of his own, with his best pirate spelling. Then they buried the box again, patting the soil flat like a careful pirate crew.

Back inside, the kitchen smelled of warm toast. Leo's mom waved a dish towel and smiled. "Did you find any treasure, pirate?" Leo grinned and yawned a huge yawn. "We found a friend's whistle, and a new treasure to keep."

Later, Leo tucked himself into bed with his hat hung on the bedpost. Rocket curled up on the rug, one ear flopping over his nose. The moon peeked through the window, soft and silver, like the whistle hidden in the shed. Leo's eyes grew heavy. Rocket let out a tiny, sleepy sigh. Outside, the apple tree rustled its leaves, hush, hush, hush. Goodnight, little pirate. Goodnight, Rocket.

first_draft.title: Pip and the Very Small Wings
first_draft.text:
Once, in a cave full of warm moss, lived a little dragon named Pip. Pip had wings the color of plums. They were big and crinkly, but Pip did not like to use them.

"Up we go!" said Mama Dragon every morning. Pip shut her eyes tight. She held onto a rock with all four claws. "Not today," she whispered. "My tummy feels wobbly."

One sunny morning, Pip's friend Tobo came swooping past. Tobo was a round green dragon who went whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. "Come and see the river from up high!" he called. "It sparkles like a spilled bowl of stars!"

Pip wanted to see the sparkles. But the edge of the cave was far, far away. "What if I fall?" she said. Her voice came out very small.

Mama Dragon sat down beside her. She smelled of cinnamon and warm stones. "Let's sit with your wings," she said. "Just sit. We don't have to fly yet."

So they sat. Pip spread one wing and then the other. She flapped them softly. Flap, flap, flap went the wings, like a sleepy moth.

Then Pip heard a plop. Tobo had landed in a puddle of mud. He sat up, blinked, and gave a surprised "Hic!" His bubbles came out in a rainbow. Pip giggled so hard she tumbled over onto her back.

"You're not very good at landing," Pip said, grinning.

"Nobody is at the very start," Tobo said with a splash. "Want to try a hop with me? Just a little hop. No more than a leaf's height."

Pip looked at the rock. She looked at the mud. Then she looked at her wings. "A leaf's height," she said. "Only a leaf."

She bent her knees. She counted. "One, two, three!" She pushed off the rock. Her wings went flap, flap, flap. Pip rose one leaf high. Then two leaves. Then she wobbled, and Tobo caught her with a soft bump of his nose.

"You did it!" cheered Mama Dragon. "Your wings know the way."

Pip landed with a little thump. Her heart went thump-thump, but it was a happy thump. "Again," she said, and this time she didn't squeeze her eyes shut.

The sun slid down behind the hills. The river turned from gold to pink to blue. Tobo yawned a big yawn, and the bubbles rose from his nose like tiny lanterns.

Pip tucked her wings close, like a warm blanket. Mama Dragon hummed low and slow. The moss was soft. The cave was quiet.

"Tomorrow," Pip whispered, "we'll see the sparkles."

Then the little dragon closed her eyes, and the stars came out to keep watch.

final.text:
Once, in a cave full of warm moss, lived a little dragon named Pip. Pip had wings the color of plums. They were big and crinkly, but Pip did not like to use them. When she thought about flying, her tummy went wibble, wobble, wibble.

"Up we go!" said Mama Dragon every morning. Pip shut her eyes tight. She held onto a rock with all four claws. "Not today," she whispered. "My tummy feels wobbly."

One sunny morning, Pip's friend Tobo came swooping past. Tobo was a round green dragon who went whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. "Come and see the river from up high!" he called. "It sparkles like a spilled bowl of stars!"

Pip wanted to see the sparkles. But the edge of the cave was far, far away, and the sky beyond it looked as wide as a whole ocean. "What if I fall?" she said. Her voice came out very small.

Mama Dragon sat down beside her. She smelled of cinnamon and warm stones. "Let's sit with your wings," she said. "Just sit. We don't have to fly yet."

So they sat. Pip spread one wing and then the other. She flapped them softly. Flap, flap, flap went the wings, like a sleepy moth.

Then Pip heard a plop. Tobo had landed in a puddle of mud. He sat up, blinked, and gave a surprised "Hic!" His bubbles came out in a rainbow. Pip giggled so hard she tumbled over onto her back, and her wings flopped out like two purple pancakes.

"You're not very good at landing," Pip said, grinning.

"Nobody is at the very start," Tobo said with a splash. He shook the mud from his ears. Flick, flick, flick. "Want to try a hop with me? Just a little hop. No more than a leaf's height."

Pip looked at the rock. She looked at the mud. Then she looked at her wings. "A leaf's height," she said. "Only a leaf."

She bent her knees. She counted. "One, two, three!" She pushed off the rock. Her wings went flap, flap, flap. Pip rose one leaf high. Then two leaves. Her tail swished, and she laughed out loud. Then she wobbled, and Tobo caught her with a soft bump of his nose.

"You did it!" cheered Mama Dragon. "Your wings know the way."

Pip landed with a little thump. Her heart went thump-thump, but it was a happy thump. "Again," she said. This time she didn't squeeze her eyes shut. She watched the moss, the mud, and the sparkling river, and she kept her eyes wide open.

The sun slid down behind the hills, slow as a sleepy snail. The river turned from gold to pink to blue. Tobo yawned a big yawn, and the bubbles rose from his nose like tiny lanterns.

Pip tucked her wings close, like a warm blanket. Mama Dragon hummed low and slow. The moss was soft. The cave was quiet.

"Tomorrow," Pip whispered, "we'll see the sparkles."

Then the little dragon closed her eyes, and the stars came out to keep watch.

first_draft.title: The Midnight Crunch Party
first_draft.text:
When the kitchen clock struck midnight, the fridge door gave a tiny sigh and swung open all by itself. Inside, the vegetables began to wiggle.

Peter the Carrot hopped onto the butter dish and tapped his orange toes. "Shall we begin?" he whispered. "The party is about to start!"

Beside him, Mrs. Broccoli fluffed up her green curls. "Oh, my florets are ready for dancing," she said. "Where is the music?"

A small, squeaky voice answered from the cheese drawer. "Here! I have the music!" It was Pip the Pea, who had squeezed himself into a shiny tin whistle. He puffed his cheeks and went, "Tweedle-deedle-doo!"

The cucumbers rolled off the shelf, bumping and bonking. "Boing, boing, bonk!" they giggled. The lettuce leaves flapped like floppy wings, and the celery stalks clicked together like tap shoes. Everyone was having the best time ever.

Then a sad sound drifted out from the back of the fridge. "Hic... hic... where is my party hat?" sniffed Onion Olive, whose papery skin was shaking. "I made it myself, with a paper cone and a yellow ribbon. Now it's gone!"

Peter scratched his orange head. "We must search the whole fridge, from the top shelf to the crispy drawer!"

So the vegetables tiptoed and wobbled and tumbled. Mrs. Broccoli peeked behind the milk carton. Pip the Pea checked under the leftover pasta. The cucumbers rolled down the sliding drawer, boing, boing, bonk, and bumped right into a pile of soft mushrooms.

"Ooh, a squishy surprise," said a mushroom, and out popped the party hat, squashed flat and a little bit dusty.

Onion Olive gasped. "My hat! It's been squished!"

Carefully, Mrs. Broccoli lifted the hat with her curly green arms. Peter helped smooth the crumpled paper with his carrot leaves, and Pip blew a gentle toot on his whistle to puff out the ribbon. Slowly, the cone sprang back into shape.

Onion Olive placed it on his head, and it wobbled, just a little. "Thank you," he said, his voice shining. "Now I can dance."

So they danced. They twirled and spun and shimmied across the cold shelves. The cheese wiggled, the peppers did a jiggly bounce, and the leftover pasta shook its spirals like confetti. The whole fridge glowed with a soft, sleepy light.

But after many dances, the bouncing grew slower. Pip's whistle went "tweedle... doo..." and then only a sigh. The cucumbers yawned, boing... bonk... and rolled gently into a corner.

Peter tucked his leaves under his chin. "I think the party is ending," he murmured. "Let's rest now."

One by one, the vegetables settled into their cozy rows. Mrs. Broccoli folded her curls like a soft green blanket. Onion Olive set his party hat on the butter dish, where it sparkled in the moonlight from the window. Pip curled up in the tin whistle, and the lettuce leaves drifted down like a sleepy quilt.

The fridge door gave a tiny, gentle click. The light dimmed to a warm glow.

In the quiet kitchen, the clock ticked softly. Tick... tock... hush.

Goodnight, little vegetables.

first_draft.title: The Lantern Moth and the Missing Button
first_draft.text:
Pim lived in a tall grey house at the edge of Mossy Hollow, where the wind hummed through the chimney like a sleepy cat. Every evening, when the stars came out one by one, a small lantern moth named Odette fluttered to the bedroom window to say goodnight.

One night Odette arrived with a worried wiggle of her antennae. "Pim, I've lost my button," she whispered. "It's round and silver, and it lights up my wings when I fly in the dark. Without it, I can't find my way home to the willow tree."

Pim sat up in bed and rubbed his eyes. "Where did you last see it?"

"Somewhere near the garden gate," said Odette. "Or maybe under the teapot. Or inside the old boot. I'm not sure."

Pim pulled on his socks, which were slightly too big and went flip-flap on the floorboards. He tiptoed down the stairs. The creaky step went eek, eek, eek, and he froze. Nobody stirred. He crept on.

In the garden, the grass was cold and damp under his toes. He crouched by the gate and sniffed the air. It smelled of rain and mint. He poked under the bench, where a snail sat in a puddle, looking very pleased with itself. "Have you seen a silver button?" Pim asked. The snail only blinked its slow eyes and kept on sliding.

Next, Pim tried the kitchen. He lifted the teapot lid. Nothing but steam and the smell of chamomile. He peeked inside the boot by the back door. Nothing but a sock with a hole in its toe and a very surprised beetle.

"Oh, bother," Pim sighed, and he sat down on the bottom step. Odette settled on his knee, her wings going soft and dim.

Then Pim noticed something. Beside the stairs sat his grandmother's old sewing basket, its lid open just a crack. He lifted the lid. Amid the spools of thread and the pincushion shaped like a hedgehog, something glinted. It was a silver button, round as a moon.

"Odette!" he whispered, holding it up. "Did you drop this in the sewing basket?"

Odette fluttered in a tiny circle. "I did! I was sitting on the lid to get a better look at the moon, and it slipped right in. Oh, Pim, how silly of me."

Pim laughed softly. "Everyone loses things sometimes. Let's get you home."

He carried her out to the garden, where the sky was thick with stars. He held the button gently while Odette climbed onto it. With a bright silver flicker, her wings began to glow, pale and steady as candlelight.

She lifted into the air, and with a soft, happy hum, she flew over the wall, toward the willow tree.

Pim walked back up the stairs, eek, eek, eek, and tucked himself under his quilt. The wind hummed through the chimney. The house settled with a sigh. Somewhere far off, a small light blinked goodnight.

Pim closed his eyes, and the stars kept watch over Mossy Hollow.

first_draft.text:
Once upon a time, on a farm with a red barn, there lived a goat named Pickles. Pickles loved hats. She loved them more than hay.

One windy morning, Pickles found a big floppy hat hanging on the fence. It was Grandpa's straw hat. She put it on her head. It slid down over her eyes. Flop! Flop! Flop!

"Maaa!" said Pickles. She trotted in a circle. The hat wobbled. The hat wiggled. The hat went flying into the mud pond.

Splish! Splosh! Pickles stared at the pond. Her hat was floating like a little boat.

A duck waddled over. "Quack, quack," said Duck. "Why is your hat swimming?"

"Because I dropped it, silly," said Pickles. "Now I need a plan."

Pickles tiptoed to the edge. She stuck out one hoof. Then another. Then she slipped. Splat! She sat right down in the mud with a big, goopy plop.

Duck laughed. "Quack-quack-HA-quack!" Then the hen laughed. Then the pig snorted and giggled, "Oink-oink-hee-hee!"

Pickles looked down at her muddy legs. She looked at the floating hat. Then she giggled too. "Maaa-ha-ha!"

All the animals gathered round. Duck paddled out. She pushed the hat with her beak. Hen flapped her wings and cheered. Pig rolled in the grass and squeaked, "Hooray!"

The hat floated back to the shore. Pickles pulled it out with her teeth. Drip, drip, drip went the muddy water.

Grandpa came walking up the path. He stopped. He rubbed his chin. "Well, now," he said. "Who's been wearing my hat?"

Pickles hung her head. Then she gave a tiny, sheepish "Maaa."

Grandpa chuckled, a big, warm rumble. He lifted the soggy hat and shook it dry. "Next time, ask first, my friend."

That evening, the moon rose over the barn. The animals curled up in the hay. Duck tucked her head under her wing. Hen fluffed her feathers. Pig snored, "Hoo-hoo-hmmm."

Pickles sat beside Grandpa's hat, safe on its hook. The hay was soft. The air was still.

Shhh, went the wind. Shhh, went the hay.

Goodnight, Pickles. Goodnight, farm.

first_draft.title: Mo the Monster and the Missing Pancakes
first_draft.text:
Under the big oak tree at the end of Pickle Lane lived a monster named Gloop. Gloop had three eyes, two fuzzy green ears, and a tummy that rumbled like a wheelbarrow full of marbles. And Gloop had one very special appetite. Gloop loved pancakes. Gloop loved socks, too, but only the fluffy ones.

One rainy Tuesday, Gloop came knocking at the kitchen window of a girl named Winnie Frump. Tap, tap, squish. "Excuse me," said Gloop, in a voice like a warm bath. "Do you happen to have any pancakes? I can smell them from all the way down the lane."

Winnie peeked out. Her grandma was standing at the stove, flipping golden pancakes with a spatula. The kitchen smelled of butter and cinnamon.

"Grandma," Winnie whispered, "there's a monster at the window, and it's hungry."

Grandma did not drop her spatula. She only raised one eyebrow. "Then we had better make enough for two," she said.

But when they carried the plate out to the porch, the pancakes were gone. Not a crumb was left. Only a small, sticky footprint sat on the doormat, and beside it lay a single striped sock.

"Oh dear," said Gloop, sitting down with a plop. "I did it again. I was so excited that I ate the whole stack before I even said hello." One of Gloop's eyes filled with a teardrop the size of a grape.

Winnie thought hard. She tapped her chin. "Maybe you need a snack that takes longer to eat," she said. "Something you have to chew slowly, like a sandwich."

"A sandwich?" Gloop's ears perked up. "What goes inside a sandwich?"

"Peanut butter, banana slices, and a little honey," said Winnie. "And you can have a sock dipped in milk, if you promise to only nibble the toes."

Gloop let out a giggle that sounded like a bubble popping in a teapot. "Toes! I promise. Toes only."

So Winnie and Grandma made a sandwich, and then another, and then one more for good measure. They set them on a blue plate beside a bowl of milk and a folded, fluffy sock. Gloop took a very, very small bite. Then another. Then a long, slow, happy chewing sound, crunch, crunch, mmmm.

"Oh my wobbly whiskers," said Gloop. "This is the best thing I have ever tasted."

The rain tapped softly on the roof. The porch light glowed like a lantern. Gloop ate slowly, one bite at a time, and every time Gloop reached the end of a sandwich, Winnie handed over another one.

When the plate was empty at last, Gloop let out a long, contented sigh. A soft purple glow rose from Gloop's tummy, and Gloop's three eyes began to droop.

"Thank you, Winnie," Gloop murmured. "Next time, I'll bring you a sock of your own."

"Thank you," whispered Winnie, yawning.

Grandma tucked a blanket around Winnie's shoulders and turned off the porch light. Outside, under the oak tree, a monster curled up with a fluffy sock tucked under one ear. The rain tapped, tap, tap, softer now, softer still.

And somewhere in the dark, a small, happy rumble went hum... hum... hum... and then, very quietly, all was still.

first_draft.title: The Ghost Who Hiccupped
first_draft.text:
The old lighthouse keeper's cottage creaked every night, and tonight it creaked louder than ever. Ethan pulled his blanket up to his chin and listened. Creak. Creak. Then a sound like a teapot sighing, long and slow: whooooo.

He held his breath. A candle flickered on the windowsill, though nobody had lit it. Its little flame bent sideways, as if something had brushed past it.

"Who's there?" Ethan whispered.

The floorboards answered with a tap, tap, tap, drifting closer to his door. Then came a small, wobbly voice from the hallway. "Hic!"

Ethan blinked. "Hic?"

"Hic! Oh, bother. Hic!"

The door swung open with a squeak, and in the doorway floated a ghost. She was pale and silvery, and she wore a nightcap that was far too big for her. Her sheet trailed behind her like a long, gauzy cloud. Every few seconds, a little puff of mist popped out of her mouth. Hic!

"I'm Mirabel," she said, looking mortified. "I was supposed to say boo. I practised it all week. But I've had the hiccups since breakfast, and every time I try to be frightening, I hiccup instead."

Ethan sat up. He couldn't help it. A giggle bubbled out of him. "Hic," he said, copying her. Mirabel's mouth fell open, and then she giggled too, and the candle flame danced merrily on the sill.

"Do you know any cures?" Mirabel asked. "Grandmother Hollow says to hold your breath and count to ten. But I can't hold my breath. I don't have any breath to hold!"

Ethan thought hard. He pictured his grandad's kitchen, where a cup of warm water always fixed everything. "A sip of water, maybe? Then you could try a silly voice, or a surprise," he suggested. "Hiccups hate surprises."

Mirabel drifted down the hall and returned with a tiny silver cup, which she held in both hands. She sipped. The cup made a soft clink against her teeth. Then she took a deep breath, puffed out her cheeks, and tried again.

"Booo!" she wailed, very loudly.

The floorboards gave a surprised squeal. Ethan jumped, then laughed until his pillow shook. "That was almost scary!"

"Almost," Mirabel sighed. "Hic."

Ethan snorted. Then he had an idea. He reached for the flashlight under his bed and switched it on. "Watch this," he said. He tapped out a silly rhythm on the lampshade. Tap-a-tap, boing-boing, clatter-clatter. Mirabel's eyes grew round. She floated closer. She started to giggle again, and the giggle turned into a tiny, startled hiccup that made her spin three times in midair.

The creaking stopped. The tapping stopped. Only the cottage settled into its gentle night-sounds: the tick of the clock, the soft hush of the sea far below.

"Mirabel," Ethan said with a yawn, "I think the house creaks because the wind slips under the boards. And the whooo is just the chimney. Grandad says it sings when the wind is cold."

Mirabel floated to the window, where the candle was burning softly. She peered out. Silver moonlight spilled over the sea, and the lighthouse beam swept across the waves, slow and steady. "Oh," she breathed. "It is only the wind, after all. And I've been frightening myself."

She drifted back, and her hiccups had faded to nothing. She tucked her sheet neatly around herself. "Goodnight, Ethan. Thank you for helping me, even though I never managed a proper boo."

"Goodnight, Mirabel," Ethan murmured. His eyelids felt heavy as warm bread.

The candle flame shrank to a small, steady glow. The lighthouse beam swept by, and then again. Creak, went the cottage, very softly now. Whooo, sang the chimney, like a lullaby.

Ethan closed his eyes. Somewhere in the hallway, a tiny hic sounded, then nothing at all.

Sleep now, little lamp. Sleep now, sea and sky.

first_draft.title: The Knight and the Wobbly Drawbridge
first_draft.text:
Once upon a time, in a castle at the very top of a green hill, there lived a knight named Sir Bartholomew Puddingfoot. He had a shiny helmet, a wooden shield painted with yellow ducks, and a sword that rang like a bell whenever he tapped it.

One morning, a letter arrived with a wax seal shaped like a snail. It said that Lady Marigold of the Misty Marsh had challenged him to a contest. Whoever could build the finest bridge across the Gurgling Brook would win a basket of honey cakes.

"A bridge!" cried Sir Bartholomew, clanking his helmet with delight. "I am very good at bridges. Mostly."

He rushed down the hill with his tools rattling in a sack. Lady Marigold was already waiting on the far bank, wearing muddy boots and a hat full of daisies. Her dog, Biscuit, wagged his tail so hard that his whole back end wiggled.

"Ready, Sir Puddingfoot?" she called. "Let the building begin!"

Sir Bartholomew tried a bridge made of logs. It wobbled. He tried a bridge made of flat stones. It sank with a sad little splosh. He tried a bridge made of his own shield, and it floated away like a yellow duck boat, quacking all the way down the brook.

"Oh dear," said Sir Bartholomew, rubbing his nose. "This is harder than I thought."

Lady Marigold sat on a rock and swung her boots. "Why don't you ask the brook what it likes?" she said with a twinkle.

Sir Bartholomew laughed, but then he stopped and listened. The water went gurgle, gurgle, bubble, plop. It was rushing and tumbling over the stones, and it seemed to be saying something.

He crouched down and watched closely. The water flowed fastest in the middle, and it curled gently around the big round boulders near the edge. The boulders stayed still, and the water just slid past them.

"Aha!" he cried. "We need something that sits strong in the middle, like a friend who doesn't mind a little splash!"

So Sir Bartholomew and Lady Marigold rolled three big round boulders into the brook, one after another. Biscuit helped by barking at each one, which was very useful, if a little loud. Then they laid a long, flat plank across the top, tied it tight with rope, and tested it with one careful hop.

Creak. Wobble. Stillness.

The plank held.

"It works!" shouted Lady Marigold, and she skipped across, with Biscuit bounding right behind her.

Sir Bartholomew followed, slowly, with his sword tucked safely under one arm. Halfway across, he stopped, and a warm smile spread over his face.

"Do you know," he said, "I think the brook helped us win after all."

Lady Marigold gave him a honey cake, and they shared it on the bank, watching the water glitter in the last of the sunshine.

The sun slipped behind the hill. The crickets began their soft, sleepy song. Biscuit curled up on a bed of daisies with a long, happy sigh. Sir Bartholomew yawned, and his shiny helmet slid down over one eye.

The brook gurgled. Bubble. Plop. Hush.

And everyone fell fast asleep.

first_draft.title: Maya and the Button Bird
first_draft.text:
On Sunday night, Maya sat on her bed and hugged her knees. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow was her first day at Pine Hill School.

"What if nobody likes me?" she whispered.

Her grandpa sat down beside her. The bed went creak, creak, creak. "Hmm," he said. "Tell me about your new school."

"I don't know anybody there," said Maya. "Everyone already has friends."

Grandpa smiled. "Every new friend starts as a stranger. Even me, once."

Maya looked at the shelf. There sat her tin of buttons, the one she had sorted by color since she was four. Red buttons. Blue buttons. Shiny gold ones.

"Can I take the tin?" she asked.

"Of course," said Grandpa. "Bring along whatever helps."

On Monday morning, Maya walked into her classroom with the tin under her arm. Her shoes went squeak, squeak on the shiny floor. Her heart went thump, thump, thump.

A boy named Oscar was building a tower of blocks. It wobbled. Plink! A block rolled under a desk.

Maya knelt down and found it. "Here you go," she said.

"Thanks," said Oscar. Then he looked at her tin. "Whoa. What's in there?"

Maya opened the lid. Clink, clatter, clink! Buttons spilled out in a rainbow.

"Can I help you build?" Maya asked. "Those blocks need a button roof."

Oscar giggled. "A button roof? That's silly!"

"Silly is my favorite," said Maya.

So they built together. Maya placed a round green button. Oscar placed a square yellow one. They stacked and sorted and tapped. Plip, plop, tap-tap. Soon a girl named Priya came over to see.

"Can I put a purple one on top?" Priya asked.

"Yes!" said Maya and Oscar at the same time.

At lunch, the three of them sat at one table. Maya's sandwich was a little squashed, but nobody minded. Priya told a joke about a sleepy goat. Oscar made a noise like a squeaky door, and everybody laughed until their tummies hurt.

When the bell rang for home, Maya felt light, like a balloon on a string.

That night, Maya sat on her bed again. Grandpa came in and creaked the bed once more.

"How was it?" he asked.

Maya yawned a big, wide yawn. "I made two friends. And we built a button roof."

"Sounds like a very good day," said Grandpa softly.

Maya snuggled under her blanket. The room grew quiet. The moon peeked in, soft and silver.

"Goodnight, tin," she whispered.

"Goodnight, buttons," whispered Grandpa.

And the buttons on the shelf glowed, and everything settled, slow and sleepy, as the night breathed in and out.

request: Our old dog Biscuit died last week and Sam misses him a lot

first_draft.title: The Biscuit-Shaped Hollow
first_draft.text:
The garden was quiet on Saturday morning. Sam stood by the back gate with his hands in his pockets, looking at the place under the apple tree where Biscuit used to nap. The grass there was greener than the rest, and it was still flat, as if someone had just stepped away.

Sam missed the thump of a tail on the kitchen floor. He missed the jingle of Biscuit's tag, and the soft sigh the old dog made every time he lay down. Most of all he missed the way Biscuit's chin rested on his sneaker when they sat on the porch steps together.

"Are you going to stand there all day?" asked Grandma Ruth, carrying a basket of muddy carrots from the vegetable patch. Her boots squelched with every step.

"I'm thinking," said Sam.

"Thinking is good work," said Grandma. "Come and help me with the carrots. Thinking goes better with something in your hands."

So Sam knelt in the damp soil beside her. He pulled up a carrot that was shaped like a crooked elbow, and he giggled. Grandma laughed too, and her laugh sounded like a kettle starting to sing.

Then Sam had an idea. He ran inside and came back with his old red ball, the one Biscuit had chewed until it squeaked, and a jar of paints from the shelf in the shed. Grandma watched him with her eyebrows raised.

"We could make a stone," Sam said. "For under the apple tree. So the grass knows who it belongs to."

Grandma nodded slowly. "That sounds like a fine idea, Sam."

They searched the garden for a flat grey stone. Sam found one near the compost bin, smooth and cool as a pond pebble. He painted it with careful brown strokes, and when he was finished, the brown blob looked a little like a dog curled up asleep, with two floppy ears and a curly tail.

Sam's lip wobbled. He sniffed hard. "It doesn't look exactly like him."

"No," said Grandma softly. "It looks like you remembering him. That's a different thing, and it's a good thing too."

Together they carried the stone to the apple tree and pressed it gently into the soft earth. A small brown bird landed on the fence, tilted its head, and sang three bright notes, as if it were saying hello.

Sam sat down on the grass beside the stone. He pulled his knees up to his chest and rested his chin on them, the way Biscuit used to rest his chin on Sam's sneaker. The grass was cool and sweet-smelling. A breeze moved the apple leaves, shush, shush, shush.

"I miss him," Sam whispered.

"I know, sweetheart," said Grandma. She sat down beside him, and her shoulder was warm against his. "Missing him is part of loving him. We can miss him together."

The sun slid behind the hills. The sky turned the color of honey, then peach, then soft violet. The bird flew away to bed, and the crickets began their gentle humming.

Sam yawned a wide, slow yawn. Grandma tucked his jacket around his shoulders, and they walked back to the house without hurrying.

Inside, the lamp was low and the kitchen smelled of carrot soup. Sam climbed into bed, and the blanket settled over him like a sleepy cloud.

Outside, the apple tree rustled once, softly. Sam closed his eyes, and the house grew quiet, and the stars came out one by one.

Good night, Sam. Good night, Biscuit.

first_draft.text:

Then she remembered her own snug hollow in the oak trunk. She flew back and peeked inside. A squirrel named Brindle was curled up there, snoring softly, with a pile of acorns tucked under her tail.

Mossbell tapped the bark gently. "Brindle? Hoo, hoo. May I rest here too?"

Brindle opened one sleepy eye. "There is room," she yawned, in a small, sleepy voice, "if we move the acorns."

Together they rolled the acorns into a little heap by the door. Thump. Bump. Roll. Brindle tucked the last one beside her. Mossbell fluffed her feathers into a cozy ring.

"Hoo, hoo, soft and slow," sang Mossbell, and her voice was as soft as feathers. Brindle yawned a yawn that sounded like a sigh.

"Hoo," whispered Mossbell.

"Hush," whispered Brindle.

Their eyes closed, one and two. The old oak rocked them gently, softly, slowly, until the whole night was still.

first_draft.title: The Glow Beneath the Hill
first_draft.text:
Zoe had three favorite things in the whole wide world: crystals, quiet afternoons, and her tortoise, Pebble. So when Grandpa Hamish said there was a cave behind the old green hill, Zoe was already pulling on her boots before he finished his sentence.

Pebble walked very slowly, one careful step at a time, as if each step needed a little thinking about. "Slow and steady," Grandpa said, tapping his walking stick on the grass. "Pebble is our best guide." Pebble did not argue. Tortoises rarely do.

The cave mouth was round and smooth, like the inside of a seashell. Cool air breathed out of it, smelling of wet moss and sleepy stone. Zoe clicked on their torch, and a yellow circle slid across the floor. "Hello!" she called. "Hel-lo... lo... lo," the cave answered softly, as if it were trying out her voice.

They walked on, past dripping ledges and puddles that wobbled like jelly. Zoe counted her steps in whispers. Seven. Eight. Nine. Then Pebble stopped, turned his wrinkly head, and tucked himself into a narrow passage on the left, where the torch beam could not reach.

"Pebble!" Zoe said. She heard a soft scrape, then nothing at all. "Grandpa, he's gone the wrong way!"

The torch gave a worried flicker. Flicker. Flicker. Then it went dim, like a candle running out of breath. Zoe's tummy did a small wobble. She remembered Grandpa's rule: stay where I can see you. He was right behind her, close enough to hear his breathing.

"Let's give our eyes a minute to wake up," Grandpa said gently. "Sometimes the dark has more to show us than we think."

Zoe took a deep breath. She switched the torch off.

At first there was only black. Then, very faintly, a glow appeared up ahead. It was blue, and then pink, and then a soft gold, like a nightlight that had been waiting just for her. Zoe's shoulders loosened.

"Grandpa," she breathed. "Look."

Holding hands, they crept along the narrow passage. It opened into a little round room, and there, sitting calmly beside the wall, was Pebble. Above him grew a cluster of crystals as tall as Zoe's shoulders, glowing from the inside like frosted lanterns. Some were lilac, some were honey-colored, and one at the very top shone the color of a summer sky. When Zoe leaned close, the whole cluster gave a tiny hum, like a spoon tapping a glass.

"Oh," Zoe whispered. "It's the most amazing thing I've ever seen."

Her fingers reached toward a small purple crystal near the bottom. It looked so lovely, and it would look so lovely on her windowsill at home. Then she stopped, her hand hovering in the glowing air.

"If I take it," she said slowly, "the cave will be a little bit darker for the next person who comes. And the other crystals might miss their friend."

Grandpa's eyes crinkled. "That's a thoughtful thing to notice. What do you think we could do instead?"

Zoe thought hard. "We could remember it. We could draw it. And we could bring our friends to see it, but only if they promise to be gentle."

So Grandpa fetched his small notebook, and Zoe sat cross-legged on a flat stone, sketching with a stubby pencil. Her drawing had too many sparkles and one wobbly tortoise, but it was the best picture she had ever made. Pebble, who had never been good at sitting still, poked his head out and nibbled a dandelion leaf that Grandpa had tucked in his pocket.

When the drawing was finished, Zoe switched the torch back on. It flickered once, then glowed steady and bright. "Come on, Pebble," she called softly. "Slow and steady, all the way home." Pebble began his careful walk, and Zoe walked beside him, counting out loud. Seven, eight, nine. The echo counted back, a little quieter each time.

Outside, the sky had turned peach and violet. The green hill looked very far away and very friendly.

"Grandpa," Zoe said, tucking the notebook under her arm, "I think the best treasures are the ones we share. And the ones we leave in their own home, so others can find them too."

"That's exactly right, sweetheart," said Grandpa, and he squeezed her hand.

That night, Zoe set Pebble on the rug and propped her drawing on the windowsill, where she could see it from her pillow. Outside, the moon was low and silver. Downstairs, a clock ticked, slow and steady. Pebble yawned, a long, slow, tortoise yawn.

Zoe pulled up her blanket and let her eyes drift closed. Somewhere under the hill, the crystals were still glowing, soft and patient, keeping their secret for the next curious friend.

Goodnight, Pebble. Goodnight, crystals. Goodnight, Zoe.
